issue_context.title: The BlockingCollection<T> backed by a custom collection doesn't work properly
comments:
> The problem is that the bounding functionality of the BlockingCollection<T> seems to brake when a duplicate item has been rejected by the underlying collection.

Such a collection can't work with `BlockingCollection<T>`.  It assumes that if `TryAdd` returns true, the item was successfully added and can later be consumed via `TryTake`.  Returning true after throwing away the item violates that.  Similarly returning false tells the `BlockingCollection<T>` that the item can't be added because there isn't sufficient room, which is erroneous for the `BlockingCollection<T>`.

> Similarly returning false tells the `BlockingCollection<T>` that the item can't be added because there isn't sufficient room, which is erroneous for the `BlockingCollection<T>`.

Hmm, that's a bit disappointing. Is there any chance that the implementation of the `BlockingCollection<T>` could be changed, so that it can handle gracefully the case that the underlying store rejected an item?

> Is there any chance that the implementation of the BlockingCollection<T> could be changed, so that it can handle gracefully the case that the underlying store rejected an item?

It doesn't know why the item was rejected.  Was it rejected because it doesn't want/like the value and it should be discarded, was it rejected because it doesn't currently have room and wants the caller to try again later, or was it rejected because it doesn't have the room and won't have the room until TryTake is called to make room.

> It doesn't know why the item was rejected.

@stephentoub I think that I have found a workaround. I changed the code of the `ConcurrentQueueNoDuplicates<T>.TryAdd` method so that it rejects an item by throwing an exception instead of returning `false`, and the problem of the reduced `BoundedCapacity` disappears ([demo](https://dotnetfiddle.net/D4kp4k)). The `queue.TryAdd(2)` returns `true` as expected. Do you have any idea if this is a good workaround, or if it breaks the `BlockingCollection<T>` in some other way?

>  Do you have any idea if this is a good workaround

I'm not following: you're throwing an exception from your IProducerConsumerCollection.TryAdd, but that exception is being eaten by BlockingCollection and it's returning false from its TryAdd?

@eiriktsarpalis yes, this is my understanding too. The `BlockingCollection<T>` class is not prepared to handle a formal rejection from the underlying collection, although interestingly it handles well an informal (exceptional) rejection.

Honestly attempting to fix this bug looks like an undertaking that's beyond my level of expertise. Messing with concurrent collections is something that I would leave to the experts!

Exactly same problem with `TryTake`, it will leave `BlockingCollection` in corrupted state. The fix is pretty simple, but it doesn't make sense to fix only for `TryAdd`

I'll submit a PR for both of them to continue discussion
